title: Review: Gas exchange; Transport

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Alveolus
items.clue: One of the millions of tiny air sacs at the ends of the bronchioles in a mammalian lung, where gas exchange takes place.

items.label: Spongy mesophyll
items.clue: The layer of loosely packed, irregularly shaped photosynthetic cells in the lower part of a leaf, separated by interconnected air spaces that open to the stomata.

items.label: Capillary
items.clue: The narrowest blood vessel, with a wall only one endothelial cell thick and a lumen so narrow that red blood cells pass through in single file.

items.label: Xylem vessel
items.clue: A continuous tube for transport of water formed from a column of cells that have died and lost their cell contents.

questions.stem: Three cubes are used to model organisms of different sizes. Their surface area-to-volume ratios are: side 1 mm, 6 mm⁻¹; side 2 mm, 3 mm⁻¹; side 4 mm, 1.5 mm⁻¹. Which conclusion is supported by these values?

options.text: The largest cube has the most surface per unit of volume, because its total surface area is the greatest.
Each doubling of the side halves the ratio, leaving proportionally less surface to supply each unit of volume.
The ratio should have stayed constant as the cubes were scaled up, so the values must contain a measurement error.
Only the fall in the ratio matters; the distance from the centre to the surface has no effect on diffusion.

questions.stem: Mammalian lungs contain a branched network of bronchioles ending in millions of alveoli. How does this branching contribute to gas exchange?

options.text: It multiplies the area of airway wall across which gases are exchanged into the blood as air travels inward.
It lets the lungs grow larger, and a larger organ must have a bigger surface for gas exchange.
It packs a very large alveolar surface, each part close to a capillary bed, into the volume of the thorax.
It houses the muscle that contracts to pump air in and out of the alveoli found at the end of every branch.

questions.stem: A person breathes out as hard as possible. What is the role of the abdominal muscles in this forced expiration?

options.text: They contract, pushing the abdominal organs up against the relaxed diaphragm so that the volume of the thorax decreases.
They relax so that the diaphragm can rise passively, and so they have no active role in forcing the air out.
They contract together with the diaphragm, which pushes upward to squeeze the air out of the lungs from below.
They have no role, because the lungs themselves contract to expel the air once the person decides to breathe out.

questions.explanation: Contraction of the abdominal muscles raises the pressure in the abdomen and forces the organs upward against the diaphragm, which has relaxed into its dome. Together with the internal intercostal muscles pulling the ribs down and in, this reduces the thorax volume and expels air.

questions.stem: A muscle receives blood through a network of thousands of capillaries rather than through a single vessel of the same total volume. What is the advantage of this arrangement for exchange?

options.text: A single wide vessel would have more wall area than thousands of narrow ones, so exchange inside it would be faster.
The total surface area of the many narrow, branching vessels is far larger, and all the blood is close to a wall.
The narrow capillaries force the blood through faster, so more oxygen is delivered to the muscle each second.
Each capillary has fenestrations, which are needed so that cells can pass out of the blood into the muscle.

questions.stem: A micrograph shows two blood vessels in transverse section. Vessel X has a wall about as thick as the diameter of its small, round lumen. Vessel Y has a wall that is very thin compared with its wide, irregular lumen. Which identification is correct?

options.text: Y is an artery, because its wide lumen carries the large volume of blood that is at high pressure.
X is a vein, because a vein needs a thick muscular wall to pump blood back towards the heart.
X is an artery, because its wall is thick relative to its lumen to withstand high pressure.
Neither can be identified, because a micrograph cannot show whether blood is oxygenated.

questions.stem: A student counts 12 beats in 10 seconds at the radial pulse. Immediately afterwards a digital heart rate monitor on the same person reads 74 beats per minute. What is the most reasonable conclusion?

options.text: The fingertip method gives 72 beats per minute but cannot be compared with the monitor, because it measures blood flow rather than heart rate.
The values agree within the error of a 10-second count, about 6 beats per minute; a 60-second count would allow a fairer comparison.
The fingertip count of exactly 72 beats per minute is precise, so the digital monitor must be reading 2 beats per minute too high.
The student must have counted at a vein instead of an artery, which gives a slightly lower reading than the monitor does.

questions.stem: A soldier standing motionless on parade for a long time feels faint, but the feeling passes as soon as she flexes her leg muscles. What is the best explanation?

options.text: Standing still removes the muscle contractions that squeeze the leg veins, so less blood returns to the heart until she moves.
Standing still tires the muscular walls of the leg veins, so they can no longer contract to pump blood up to the heart.
Standing still stops the valves in the leg veins from opening and shutting, so they no longer push blood up to the heart.
Standing still stops the artery walls from contracting, so blood can no longer be pumped from the heart to the brain.

questions.stem: Illustrative data. In a study of 20 countries, the correlation coefficient between mean saturated fat intake and the death rate from coronary heart disease was +0.85. What can be concluded from this result alone?

options.text: Saturated fat in the diet is shown to cause coronary heart disease, because the coefficient is so close to +1, the maximum.
The relationship is weak, because a correlation calculated from only 20 countries cannot be a strong one.
There is a strong positive correlation between the variables, but this does not prove that one causes the other.
Saturated fat from food coats the inside of the coronary arteries, which is why the two variables rise together in step.

questions.stem: In a tall tree the column of water in the xylem is under considerable tension, yet it does not break into separate lengths with gaps between them. Which property of water explains this?

options.text: Water molecules are attracted to the lignin of the vessel wall, which holds each part of the column in place.
Water molecules are held to one another by hydrogen bonds, so the whole column moves as an unbroken unit.
Water is pushed steadily upwards from the roots, so the column is kept under compression, not tension.
Water molecules are pulled upwards by active transport in the xylem, faster than any gaps could form.

questions.stem: A xylem vessel in a leaf vein is blocked by an air bubble. Water still reaches the leaf cells beyond the blockage. Which feature of xylem makes this possible?

options.text: Living xylem cells actively transport water around the blockage using ATP from respiration.
The lignified side walls are completely sealed, so water can only move through the open ends.
The end walls of the vessel are absent, so water is pushed past the bubble from below.
Pits in the lignified walls let water pass sideways into a neighbouring vessel.
